Benefits and Harms of SGLT2 Inhibitors in Type 2 Diabetes

Storgaard H, Gluud LL, Bennett C, et al. PLOS ONE. 2016;11(11):e0166125.

Scope warning. This is a 2016 synthesis focused mainly on glycaemic efficacy, metabolic effects, and short-to-medium-term harms at maximal approved doses. It predates much of the later cardiovascular, heart-failure, and kidney-outcome evidence that now dominates SGLT2-inhibitor clinical positioning. It should not be used alone to make a current formulary decision.

One-page synthesis

Verdict: Skim deeply. High value for understanding early class-level efficacy/safety evidence and the limitations of the pre-outcomes-trial evidence base; lower value as a stand-alone guide to current formulary interchangeability.

The review identified 42 double-blind RCTs (59 reports; 24,500 participants) evaluating canagliflozin 300 mg/day, dapagliflozin 10 mg/day, or empagliflozin 25 mg/day for at least 12 weeks. Versus placebo, SGLT2 inhibitors lowered HbA1c by 0.69 percentage points (95% CI 0.62–0.75 lower; 34 RCTs, n=9,154), with substantial heterogeneity and evidence of small-study effects. Versus oral antidiabetic comparators, the pooled HbA1c difference was -0.20 percentage points (95% CI -0.28 to -0.13), driven by larger differences versus sulfonylureas and DPP-4 inhibitors than versus metformin.

Secondary pooled effects favored SGLT2 inhibitors for body weight and blood pressure, with small lipid changes. Genital tract infection showed the clearest harm signal (versus placebo RR 4.34, 95% CI 3.35–5.63); urinary tract infection was modestly higher (RR 1.14, 95% CI 1.00–1.30). Serious adverse events did not differ in the main-text placebo analysis (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.87–1.12), but serious outcomes were uncommon, several estimates were very imprecise, adverse-event reporting was inconsistent, and every included trial was industry funded. The review graded the primary placebo HbA1c evidence low quality because of heterogeneity and small-study/publication-bias concerns.

Methods and evidence architecture

Eligibility and search

Eligible studies were English-language, double-blind RCTs in adults with type 2 diabetes, duration ≥12 weeks, using the maximal approved daily doses of canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, or empagliflozin. Eligible comparators were placebo, metformin, sulfonylureas, or DPP-4 inhibitors with equal background therapy permitted. Trials restricted to impaired kidney function, Japan-only trials under the protocol rules, and unapproved/discontinued agents were excluded.

The authors searched the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Science Citation Index, and the WHO trial-search database, supplemented by manual searching and additional data obtained from investigators, manufacturers, and the Yale Open Data Access project. The search was updated in October 2015. The protocol was prospectively registered (CRD42014008960), and the supplied PRISMA checklist documents reporting against PRISMA 2009.

Extraction and analysis

Study selection was performed independently by two reviewers, outcome extraction by three authors, and disagreements were resolved by consensus. Longest available treatment-period data were used. SGLT2-versus-placebo and SGLT2-versus-oral-drug analyses were separated. Risk of bias used Cochrane domains and evidence certainty used GRADE.

Random-effects meta-analysis was planned because heterogeneity was expected; continuous outcomes used mean differences and dichotomous outcomes risk ratios with 95% CIs. Heterogeneity was evaluated with I², drug/comparator subgroup analyses were performed, and small-study effects were tested when at least ten trials were available.

Results

Study selection and bias

The review screened 780 deduplicated records, assessed 76 full texts, and included 42 studies (59 reports). The supplementary trial-characteristics file provides detailed study-level design and risk-of-bias data. Randomization, concealment, and blinding were generally rated low risk, but other bias remained unclear because all trials were industry funded; no trial was low risk across every domain.

Table 2 and prose also disagree on the fasting-plasma-glucose representation and the sign of the triglyceride CI upper bound. These discrepancies are preserved rather than silently harmonized.

Figures, tables, and supplements

Figure 1 — study flow

Structured reading: 1,087 database records plus 20 other records; 780 after deduplication; 704 excluded at screening; 76 full texts assessed; 17 full texts excluded; 42 studies in 59 reports entered quantitative synthesis.

Figure 2 — HbA1c versus placebo

The overall pooled effect is -0.69 percentage points. Canagliflozin shows the largest subgroup estimate (-0.85), with dapagliflozin (-0.60) and empagliflozin (-0.69) also favoring active therapy.

Figure 3 — HbA1c versus oral antidiabetic drugs

The pooled comparison favors SGLT2 inhibitors by -0.20 percentage points; metformin is essentially neutral, while sulfonylurea and DPP-4 inhibitor comparisons favor SGLT2 inhibitors modestly.

Supplementary risk-of-bias figures

The study-level and domain-summary visuals support the authors’ conclusion that core randomization/blinding domains were usually low risk, while allocation concealment was often unclear and “other bias” was unclear across the evidence base.

Evaluation and appraisal

Relevance: 8/10
Directly relevant to class-level SGLT2 efficacy/safety and formulary rationale.
Limit: predates modern cardiorenal outcomes evidence.
Novelty: 7/10
At publication, provided broad pooled class and drug-subgroup evidence across 42 RCTs.
Limit: contribution is now historical.
Method strength: 7/10
Prospective protocol, broad search, independent review, Cochrane RoB, GRADE, random-effects synthesis.
Limit: dose restrictions, heterogeneity, secondary-source reliance for trial details.
Evidence strength: 6/10
Strong signal for glycaemic/weight/BP effects and genital infection; serious clinical outcomes remain underpowered.
Limit: low GRADE for primary placebo HbA1c, small-study effects, inconsistent harms reporting.
External validity: 6/10
Large multinational RCT base.
Limit: research settings, selected populations, maximal doses, renal-impaired populations excluded.
Implementation value: 6/10
Useful background for class-effect and early safety discussions.
Limit: insufficient alone for a 2026 formulary substitution decision.

Strengths

Prospective registration, explicit eligibility, broad database search, independent study selection/extraction, manufacturer/YODA data supplementation, formal risk-of-bias assessment, GRADE, and transparent supporting files materially improve traceability. The supplied supplement package is unusually useful for auditability.

Limitations

The evidence base shows substantial heterogeneity for central efficacy outcomes, small-study effects, universal industry funding of included trials, and sparse serious clinical events. Several safety outcomes have very wide confidence intervals, ketoacidosis was not routinely reported, and the review itself contains minor denominator/CI/unit inconsistencies between narrative and supplements. The selected maximal-dose design narrows dose-level generalizability.

Most importantly for current use, this 2016 evidence package does not answer the modern question of comparative cardiovascular, heart-failure, and kidney protection across individual SGLT2 inhibitors. Later outcome trials and current guidelines are required before making present-day practice or formulary conclusions.

Implementation / practice takeaways

Use it for
Historical class-effect evidence for HbA1c, body weight, BP, genital infection, and comparison with metformin/SU/DPP-4 inhibitors.
Do not use it for
Current therapeutic interchangeability, current cardiorenal indications, inpatient initiation/continuation policy, or contemporary renal thresholds.
Formulary signal
The review supports broad glycaemic class efficacy but does not demonstrate equivalence of individual agents on modern patient-centered cardiorenal outcomes.
